primary_cause: No material HD-specific negative Mar 9-12. Repricing of discretionary retail and housing-sensitive exposure on severe recession fears
secondary_factors: Broad risk-off liquidation. Concern foot traffic supply chains and big-ticket home-improvement demand would weaken. Reuters: U.S. manufacturing nearly stalled
store_description: HD's 10.5% drop looks mainly like a macro-driven selloff in a consumer-cyclical retailer as the market absorbed the March 11 pandemic declaration and March 12 ECB-related stress. No meaningful Home Depot-specific bad news in the prior three days.

primary_cause: Financial-sector repricing from recession risk plus fast collapse in rates and credit sentiment. ECB disappointment worsened global credit stress
secondary_factors: Marketwide liquidity stress on March 12. Concern about trading counterparty underwriting activity and investment-banking slowdown. No major Goldman-specific negative
store_description: GS fell 12.3% largely because the market was aggressively marking down capital-markets and credit-sensitive financials as COVID shock effects intensified and policymakers failed to calm markets on March 12.

primary_cause: Fear of sudden ad-spending slowdown as travel local commerce and SME demand collapsed. Google canceled I/O event. Mar 11 banned face-mask ads globally
secondary_factors: General mega-cap tech de-risking. Analyst estimate: travel-search ad revenue could fall ~$1B Q1 ~$3B Q2. Subsequent reporting confirms March was when strong first two months gave way to significant slowdown
store_description: Both share classes dropped just over 8% as investors rapidly repriced Alphabet's exposure to advertising especially after COVID was declared a pandemic and travel restrictions hit major ad categories.

primary_cause: Same as GOOGL. Fear of ad-spending weakness especially travel ads. Ad-market deterioration and travel-search spending risk
secondary_factors: Mega-cap tech de-risking. Estimates: ~$1B less travel-search ad spend Q1 ~$3B less Q2. Broader U.S. ad-market hit ~$26B
store_description: GOOG fell for the same reason GOOGL did: investors were rapidly discounting lower ad demand especially in travel one of Google's most important advertiser verticals.

primary_cause: Anticipation of deep auto demand slump and coming factory interruptions. No major company-specific formal shutdown announcement before Mar 12. GM did not announce North America production suspension until Mar 18
secondary_factors: Europe travel restrictions. General recession panic. Supply-chain fears. Later-confirmed plant shutdown risk
store_description: GM's 11.4% decline was primarily a forward-looking auto-sector repricing as investors anticipated both a sales collapse and manufacturing disruptions before the official shutdowns were announced. The market was effectively discounting what became explicit on March 18.

primary_cause: No negative Gilead-specific headline Mar 9-12. Remdesivir still viewed as potential treatment candidate. Broad biotech and pharma de-risking with market crash
secondary_factors: Profit-taking after earlier remdesivir optimism. Rotation out of even defensive names during forced liquidation. Negative leaked WHO trial episode came later in April
store_description: GILD fell less than many cyclicals which fits the absence of clear company-specific bad news and the stock's relative support from remdesivir optionality. The most plausible explanation is broad market liquidation overwhelming a name that otherwise had some COVID-related upside narrative.

primary_cause: Sharp repricing of GE Aviation and cyclical industrial exposure amid collapse in air travel and industrial demand expectations. Oil ~25% plunge Mar 9
secondary_factors: Balance-sheet sensitivity. GE reputation as higher-risk industrial. No GE-specific Mar 9-12 corporate warning. Aviation power and industrial demand all vulnerable
store_description: GE's 11.9% drop was most likely driven by the market's realization that an accelerating travel shutdown and recession would hammer GE Aviation and broader industrial demand. Severe sector-exposure repricing.

primary_cause: Business-jet and cyclical aerospace exposure especially Gulfstream overwhelmed the stock. Travel shock worsened outlook for business aviation
secondary_factors: Broad industrial and defense de-risking. Recession panic. No major GD-specific negative headline
store_description: GD's nearly 11% decline looks less like a defense-spending story and more like a sudden markdown of Gulfstream and capital-goods exposure as travel restrictions and recession fears intensified.

primary_cause: No IBM-specific negative Mar 9-12. Fear of weaker enterprise spending and services demand in fast-moving recession
secondary_factors: Broad tech selloff. Credit and liquidity stress. Cyclical IT exposure. Abrupt reassessment of enterprise IT spending consulting demand and legacy tech exposure
store_description: IBM's 12.9% drop appears driven mainly by recession pricing against consulting infrastructure and enterprise software and services budgets rather than a fresh IBM-specific headline.

primary_cause: No material Salesforce-specific negative Mar 9-12. Repricing of enterprise-software demand risk
secondary_factors: General tech de-risking and broad market liquidation. Potential slowing enterprise software spending and delayed customer commitments
store_description: CRM's 9% drop looks like investors discounting weaker near-term bookings and IT budget caution rather than reacting to a company-specific shock. COVID escalation quickly shifted the market from growth at any price to balance-sheet and near-term cash-flow survival.

primary_cause: Industrial recession and capex-demand fears. Reuters manufacturing coverage showed U.S. factory activity stalling and supply chains being hit
secondary_factors: Supply-chain strain. Broad industrial selling. No Mar 9-12 Emerson-specific announcement
store_description: EMR's 11.4% fall was most likely the market marking down industrial automation and process end-markets for a sharper global slowdown. With no clear Emerson-specific negative headline the strongest explanation is deteriorating factory and capital-spending expectations.

primary_cause: No Duke-specific negative. Forced liquidation and indiscriminate market stress. Utilities liquidated in violent cross-asset dash for cash despite lower rates
secondary_factors: Concern that commercial and industrial power demand would weaken in a shutdown recession
store_description: DUK's 11.5% decline is one of the clearer examples of March 12 becoming indiscriminate: even defensive utilities were sold hard as liquidity stress and panic overwhelmed fundamentals. No Duke-specific catalyst in the prior three days.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters Mar 12 reported Disney would close California and Florida parks and Paris resort through month-end. Clear stock-specific trigger
secondary_factors: Travel ban. Looming cruise and box-office disruption. Rapidly worsening outlook for parks resorts and adjacent businesses
store_description: DIS dropped 13.0% because investors suddenly had a concrete estimate of revenue loss: Disney said on March 12 it would shut Disneyland Walt Disney World and Disneyland Paris through month-end. That transformed COVID from a vague macro threat into a direct earnings shock for parks resorts and adjacent businesses.

primary_cause: No Danaher-specific negative Mar 9-12. Broad market liquidation. Healthcare and life-sciences exposure more defensive than industrials
secondary_factors: Temporary uncertainty around hospital and procedure volumes and M&A integration risk. Smaller drawdown relative to deep cyclicals
store_description: DHR's 7.5% decline looks mostly like marketwide de-risking rather than a company-specific negative event. Relative to industrial cyclicals the smaller drawdown is consistent with Danaher's more defensive life-sciences profile.

primary_cause: Anticipated drop in farm-equipment demand and industrial activity. Rapid worsening macro outlook for farm incomes equipment purchases and industrial demand
secondary_factors: Supply-chain disruptions. Broad machinery and industrial selling. No Deere-specific negative Mar 9-12
store_description: DE's 10.6% fall was most likely a cyclical-industrials repricing: investors were discounting weaker farmer spending tighter credit and possible production and logistics disruptions. No Deere-specific headline in the prior three days strong enough to explain the move on its own.

primary_cause: Collapse in crude prices from Saudi-Russia price war plus demand fears from COVID. Reuters Mar 9 oil plunged ~25%
secondary_factors: Broad equity-market panic. Concerns about energy capex and cash flow
store_description: CVX's 8.2% drop was primarily tied to the dual shock of a crude-price collapse and a fast worsening demand outlook. When oil fell about 25% on March 9 the market began aggressively revaluing the earnings and balance-sheet outlook for integrated oil majors and March 12 extended that repricing.

primary_cause: No major CVS-specific negative Mar 9-12. Broad liquidation plus concern over Aetna exposure and healthcare-services and recession mix
secondary_factors: Pressure on consumer health spending mix. Broad balance-sheet and cross-sector derisking. Too large to be explained by stock-specific news
store_description: CVS's 10.9% decline seems too large to be explained by stock-specific news because no meaningful CVS or Aetna headline was found in the exact lookback window. The more plausible explanation is that March 12's forced selling engulfed managed-care and healthcare-services names despite their defensive elements.

primary_cause: Fear of weaker networking hardware demand and supply-chain disruption. Directly exposed to enterprise and service-provider capex plus supply-chain risk
secondary_factors: General tech selloff and enterprise spending risk. Reuters and ISM survey evidence showing supply-chain disruption. No Cisco-specific bad headline Mar 9-12
store_description: CSCO's 10.4% drop appears driven by a rapid reassessment of global IT hardware demand and supply continuity rather than a discrete Cisco announcement. As the market shifted from temporary virus disruption to global recession mature hardware names were hit hard.

primary_cause: Repricing of global shipping and logistics volumes as trade and mobility froze. Acutely exposed to international transport disruption especially Europe-related flows after travel restriction
secondary_factors: Broad cyclical selloff. Recession fears. Concerns about TNT Europe exposure. No FedEx-specific formal warning Mar 9-12
store_description: FDX's 12.6% decline was most likely driven by the market pricing in a severe contraction in cross-border shipments and business activity especially after the U.S. restricted travel from much of Europe on March 11.

primary_cause: Acute financial-system stress. Mar 15 Fed slashed rates to 0-0.25% and restarted large-scale asset purchases. Market read Fed emergency move as confirmation conditions deteriorating extremely fast
secondary_factors: Collapsing rates hurting bank profitability. Counterparty and credit concerns. General panic. Reuters: large U.S. banks planned to use Fed discount window underscoring funding stress
store_description: MS's 15.6% drop on March 16 was driven by the market reading the Fed's emergency Sunday cut to zero not as a cure but as confirmation that conditions were deteriorating extremely fast. For broker-dealers and banks that meant pressure on funding credit deal activity and rate-sensitive earnings all at once.
